extracted.intended_audience: federal district court judges and jurors in patent infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions describing claim construction, claim interpretation, means-/step-plus-function rules, and the elements and limitations of various forms of patent infringement (direct literal, doctrine of equivalents, inducement, contributory, and §271(f) foreign-supply theories). Intended to guide jury findings on infringement and related issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim language defines scope
rubrics_metrics.description: By understanding the meaning of the words in a claim and by understanding that the words in a claim set forth the requirements that a product or process must meet in order to be covered by that claim, you will be able to understand the scope of coverage for each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you understand what each claim covers, you are prepared to decide issues such as infringement and invalidity. (Implied: compare accused product/process to claim requirements to determine coverage.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase meanings (comprising/consisting of/consisting essentially of)
rubrics_metrics.description: The document explains the different transition phrases used in claims: 'comprising' is open-ended and allows additional steps; 'consisting of' is closed-ended meaning 'I claim what follows and nothing else'; 'consisting essentially of' is a middle ground between 'comprising' and 'consisting of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities and case citations illustrate how these transitions affect claim scope (e.g., Cook Biotech, Invitrogen, Conoco, Vehicular Techs., CIAS, AK Steel). Apply the appropriate transition meaning when comparing accused product/process to the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent vs. dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'independent claim' sets forth all of the requirements that must be met in order to be covered by that claim. A 'dependent claim' does not recite all requirements itself but refers to another claim, incorporating that claim's requirements and adding its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine what a dependent claim covers, it is necessary to look at both the dependent claim and any other claim(s) to which it refers. A dependent claim includes all requirements of the claim(s) to which it refers plus additional requirements. (Note: It may be helpful to submit to the jury a chart setting forth all dependencies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's claim constructions control
rubrics_metrics.description: The court will explain the meaning of some words of the claims and the jury must accept the court's definition of these words as correct. For words not defined by the court, apply their common meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's definitions should not be taken as indicating how the jury should decide issues like infringement or invalidity — those are for the jury to decide. Claim-by-claim sub-instructions may be provided if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function / Step-plus-function (§112, ¶6) — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'means for [function]' or 'step for [function]' phrase has a special meaning: it does not cover all structures/acts that could perform the function, but instead covers a structure (or set of structures) or acts that perform that function and that are identical or 'equivalent' to the structure(s)/act(s) described in the patent for performing that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will identify the structures/acts described in the patent that perform the function; those identifications should be applied like any other claim-term definition. The issue of whether two structures/acts are identical or equivalent is for the jury to decide; the judge will later explain how to determine 'equivalence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Means/step-plus-function literal infringement test
rubrics_metrics.description: A product/process meets a means/step-plus-function claim requirement if (1) it has a structure/set of structures or action/set of actions that perform the identical function recited in the claim, and (2) that structure/set of structures or action/set of actions is identical or 'equivalent' to one or more of the described structure(s)/action(s) from the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the product does not perform the specific function, it does not literally infringe. If it performs the function but the structure/action is not identical or equivalent to the disclosed structure/act, it does not literally infringe. Equivalence requires that differences were insubstantial or that they perform substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, and that interchangeability was known to persons of ordinary skill at the time the patent issued. Equivalence cannot embrace technology developed after issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement assessed claim-by-claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is assessed on a claim-by-claim basis; there may be infringement as to one claim but not another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee must prove infringement of one or more claims by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Compare the accused product/process to each and every claim requirement to determine whether all requirements of that claim are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five types of infringement to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five possible ways that a claim may be infringed: (1) direct infringement; (2) active inducement; (3) contributory infringement; (4) infringement through the supply of components from the United States to another country; and (5) infringement through importation of a product made abroad by a patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active inducement and contributory infringement are indirect infringement and cannot exist without someone else engaging in direct infringement. The jury will be instructed on each type in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal direct infringement — element-by-element rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove direct literal infringement, the patentee must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused made, used, sold, offered for sale within, or imported into the U.S. a product or process that meets all of the requirements of a claim without permission during the patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must compare the accused product/process with each and every one of the claim's requirements. If any claim element is missing, there is no literal infringement. Dependent-claim logic: if an independent claim is not infringed, dependent claims that refer to it cannot be infringed; if an independent claim is infringed, you still must decide separately whether dependent claims are also infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — general test
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the accused product/process does not literally meet all claim requirements, it can infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if it contains elements or performs steps corresponding to each and every claim requirement that are equivalent to the claimed requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An element or step is equivalent if a person of ordinary skill would have considered the differences insubstantial, or would have found that the structure/action: (1) performs substantially the same function, (2) in substantially the same way, (3) to achieve substantially the same result. Interchangeability must have been known to a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time; present-day interchangeability alone is insufficient. Equivalence must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on doctrine of equivalents — prior art / obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art may preclude a finding of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. The jury must determine what products/processes are in the prior art and what would have been obvious from the prior art to a person of ordinary skill at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the alleged equivalent feature was in the prior art or would have been obvious, you must find no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. The patentee of the hypothetical equivalent claim must be shown by the alleged infringer by a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on doctrine of equivalents — patent disclosure preclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not find equivalence if the allegedly equivalent alternative feature was described somewhere in the patent and the accused product/process is not covered literally by any claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent disclosure of the alternative can preclude finding that the alternative is an equivalent to an unmet claim requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel (argument- and amendment-based) constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may be estopped from asserting equivalence where, during prosecution, the applicant distinguished the unmet requirement from the allegedly equivalent alternative or amended claims in a way that surrendered scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For amendment-based estoppel, to find equivalents despite an amendment you must find one or more factors such as: (1) the amendment substituted a broader requirement for a narrower one or replaced equal scope; (2) the reason for the amendment was unrelated to patentability; (3) a person of ordinary skill at the time of amendment would not have foreseen substitution of the allegedly equivalent alternative; (4) the amendment was tangential; or (5) other reasons (e.g., shortcomings of language) prevented claiming the alternative. If none apply, equivalence may be precluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitiation limitation on equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not determine that an alternative aspect of a product/process is equivalent to an unmet requirement if a finding of equivalence would effectively eliminate that requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The alleged equivalent cannot eliminate or ignore an element or requirement of the claim (i.e., cannot 'vitiate' the claim element).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — active inducement elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Active inducement exists only if the patentee proves by a preponderance of the evidence: (1) acts are actually carried out by another who directly infringes; (2) the alleged inducer took action intending to cause the infringing acts by that other; and (3) the alleged inducer was aware of the patent and knew the acts, if taken, would constitute infringement (or believed there was a high probability and took deliberate steps to avoid learning of that infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the alleged inducer believed the encouraged acts did not infringe, they cannot be liable for inducement. Mere knowledge that there was a substantial risk is insufficient; specific intent to induce or willful blindness is required. Proof is by preponderance of the evidence. Committee comments note inclusion of willful blindness language only when at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — contributory infringement elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement exists if the patentee proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) the alleged infringer sells/offers/imports a component of a product or apparatus for use in a process during the patent term; (2) the component has no substantial noninfringing use; (3) the component constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) the alleged infringer is aware of the patent and knows that the component's only substantial use may be covered by a claim or satisfy a claim under the doctrine of equivalents; and (5) that use directly infringes the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of the above requirements must be proved by a preponderance of the evidence. Case law (35 U.S.C. §271(c), Aro, Ricoh, etc.) provides context such as 'not a staple article' concept and knowledge requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: §271(f)(1) — supply-from-U.S. for foreign combination (active inducement) elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §271(f)(1), the patentee must prove by a preponderance that: (1) the alleged infringer supplies (or causes to be supplied) components from the United States to a place outside the U.S. that make up all or a substantial portion of the invention claimed; (2) the alleged infringer intentionally took action to cause another outside the U.S. to assemble the components; (3) the alleged infringer knew of the patent and knew the encouraged acts constitute infringement; and (4) the encouraged acts would constitute direct infringement if carried out in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the alleged infringer believed the acts it encouraged would not constitute infringement if carried out in the U.S., it cannot be liable under §271(f)(1). Specific intent to cause assembly abroad and knowledge of the patent are required; proof is by preponderance of the evidence.
